title: Unit 3 : Session 8 : SLO 1 — Non-Restoring Division Algorithm
sections: Section A: Match the Following (Remember)
A. Non-Restoring Division → 3. No restoration; handled in next cycle
B. Shift Left Operation → 2. Moves remainder and quotient bits to the left
C. Negative Partial Remainder → 1. Adds divisor if the remainder is negative
D. Quotient Bit = 0 → 4. Indicates subtraction failed
E. Positive Partial Remainder → 5. Indicates subtraction succeeded
Section B: Fill in the Blanks (Understand)
Non-restoring division removes the need for the RESTORATION step found in restoring division.
If the partial remainder is negative, the divisor is ADDED in the next step.
The algorithm uses an initial SHIFT of the remainder and quotient registers.
The QUOTIENT bit is set to 0 when the partial remainder is negative.
The division result consists of the QUOTIENT and the final remainder.
Section C: Simulate the Algorithm (Apply): 0100 (4) ÷ 0010 (2)
Final correction: A < 0 → A = A + M = 1110 + 0010 = 0000
Final Quotient = 0010 (2), Remainder = 0000 (0)   (4 ÷ 2 = 2 remainder 0 ✓)
Section D: Role-Play Debrief (Analyze)

More efficient than restoring because the extra restore (add-back) step inside every failed cycle is eliminated — each cycle performs exactly one add or subtract, so the loop is shorter and faster in hardware.
The end correction is needed because if the last partial remainder is negative it does not represent a valid remainder; adding the divisor once restores the true remainder.

In restoring division the quotient bit is decided after the restore check; in non-restoring the quotient bit is set directly from the sign of the partial remainder (1 if non-negative, 0 if negative) without restoring first.
